<p align='center'><b>GIT TRAINING GUIDE</b></p>
*A 15-minute introduction for new team members*  
*Includes enhanced explanations, PDF‑friendly diagrams, and step‑by‑step examples*

---

# 1. Introduction: What Git Is and Why Teams Use It
Git is a **distributed version control system**. Every developer has a full local copy of the repository, which makes everyday operations fast and reliable. Git enables teams to:

- Track changes to files over time (complete history)
- Collaborate safely without overwriting each other's work
- Create **branches** for features and fixes, then merge when ready
- Revert or roll back changes if needed

**Key idea:** Work locally, commit locally, then synchronize with a shared **remote** (e.g., GitHub, Azure Repos, Bitbucket) when ready.

<!--   -->
# 2. Core Git Terminology (The Git “Language”)
- **Repository (repo):** Project folder tracked by Git, including history in the hidden `.git/` directory.
- **Working Directory:** The files you edit on disk.
- **Staging Area (Index):** A preparation area where you collect changes for the next commit.
- **Commit:** A snapshot of staged changes with a message.
- **Branch:** A movable pointer to a commit; separate line of development.
- **Merge:** Combine changes from one branch into another, creating a merge commit (or a fast‑forward if possible).
- **Remote:** A shared server copy of the repository (e.g., `origin`).
- **Clone:** Create a local copy from a remote repository.
- **Fetch / Pull / Push:** Download new commits (`fetch`), download and integrate (`pull`), or upload local commits (`push`).
- **HEAD:** Your **current position** — the branch and latest commit your working directory reflects (explained in detail in Section 8).

# 3. How Git Works — The File Lifecycle
Git tracks a file through three major states: untracked, staged, and committed. The diagram below shows how files move from being untracked, to staged, to committed in the repository. After the diagram, we summarize the lifecycle commands.

```

+------------------+
|    UNTRACKED     |
+------------------+
( Git does not track this file yet )
       |
       v
+------------------+
|      STAGED      |
+------------------+
( File selected to be included in commit )
       |
       v
+------------------+
|    COMMITTED     |
+------------------+
( Saved permanently into project history )

```

**Commands that move files through the lifecycle:**
- `git status` — See which files are untracked, modified, or staged
- `git add <file>` — Stage changes (move to the Staging Area)
- `git commit -m "message"` — Record a snapshot of staged changes

Tips:
- Use `.gitignore` to exclude files/folders from version control
- Use `git stash` to temporarily put aside uncommitted work

# 4. Git Architecture (Local & Remote)

Git organizes your project into **three local areas (“trees”)** and one **remote repository**.  
The remote repository is conceptually the “Cloud,” and is used for collaboration, synchronization, and as the authoritative shared version of the project.

Each “tree” serves a unique purpose in Git’s workflow. Understanding how they relate — and how Git commands move data between them — is central to mastering Git.

---

# 4.1 The Local Trees

Git’s three local “trees” work together to provide a safe, structured workflow.


## Working Directory  
Your real project folder — the only tree the user can directly edit.

- You create, delete, and modify files here.
- Any edits remain untracked or modified until staged.
- Represents the **caterpillar phase** of your changes: alive, evolving, not yet saved.

This is your **active workspace**, the only place where actual file editing happens.


## Staging Area (Butterfly)

The Staging Area (Index) marks which changes will be included in the next commit.

- When you run `git add`, you “tag” or **mark** a change as ready.
- Staging is like the **butterfly** landing on a branch: the file has transformed and is now prepared to *take flight* as a commit.
- Only staged changes become part of the next snapshot.
- Staging enables carefully crafted, intentional commits.

This tree is your **commit‑preparation zone** — the precise set of changes ready to fly into history.


## Local Repository  
The `.git` database storing all commits, branches, merges, and history.

- A protected, permanent archive of everything committed.
- Stores the **flight path** — all past commits created from your butterfly (staged changes).
- You cannot edit it directly; Git updates it via commits, merges, rebases, etc.

Think of it as your **local time machine** — a complete record of your project’s evolution.


## Remote Repository (Cloud)

The shared version of the repository hosted in the Cloud (GitHub, GitLab, Azure Repos, etc.).

- Team members push their history here.
- You download others’ changes from here.
- CI/CD and automation often run from the remote.
- Remote branches (e.g., `origin/main`) mirror your cloud history.

The Remote Repository is your **team’s source of truth**.

# 4.2 Architecture Diagram (Improved, PDF‑Safe)

```
                   ( Cloud )
====================================================

   [ Local Repository ]           [ Remote Repository ]
------------------------------------------------------

                      [ Working Directory ]
```

This diagram shows the conceptual structure:

- **Cloud**: Remote repository hosting your shared project.
- **Local Repository**: Your own copy of project history.
- **Working Directory**: Where you actually edit files.
- Data moves *between* these boxes using Git commands — never inside them.

---

# 4.3 How Git Commands Move Data Between Trees

Each command interacts with one or more trees. The patterns below match the document’s diagram style and are PDF‑safe.

## Download new commits into Remote Repository

`git fetch` downloads new commits from the cloud and updates your local mirror of the remote repository. It does not change your working files or local commit history.

```bash
git fetch
```

```
cloud
  |
  o   Remote Repository
```

- Working Directory: **unchanged**
- Local Repository: **unchanged**
- Remote Repository: **updated remote‑tracking refs** (e.g., `origin/main`)

## Update Local Repository and Working Directory

`git pull` fetches new commits and then integrates them into your current branch, updating both local history and your working files.

```bash
git pull
```

```
Remote Repository
        |
        o   Local Repository
        |
        o   Working Directory
```

- Remote Repository: **unchanged**
- Local Repository: **new commits added**
- Working Directory: **files updated to latest**

## Move history into Working Directory

`git checkout` switches your branch (or restores files), rewriting the Working Directory from the Local Repository.

```bash
git checkout <branch-or-commit>
```

```
Local Repository
        |
        o   Working Directory
```

- Local Repository: **unchanged**
- Working Directory: **rewritten to selected commit/branch**

## Save staged changes into Local Repository

`git commit` writes the staged snapshot from the Working Directory into the Local Repository as a new commit.

```bash
git commit -m "message"
```

```
Working Directory
        |
        o   Local Repository
```

- Working Directory: **unchanged** (after commit)
- Local Repository: **new commit recorded**

## Upload commits to Cloud

`git push` sends your local commits to the remote repository in the cloud so others can pull them.

```bash
git push
```

```
Local Repository
        |
        o   Remote Repository
        |
        o   cloud
```

- Local Repository: **unchanged**
- Remote Repository: **updated to include your commits**
- Cloud: **reflects new remote state**


# 4.4 The Critical Concept

### ⭐ **Only the Working Directory is editable.** ⭐

Everything else is history or storage:

- Local Repository = your committed history  
- Remote Repository = cloud copy of history  
- Working Directory = your editable project files  

All Git operations revolve around moving data **into or out of** the Working Directory.

```
EDIT HERE → STAGE → COMMIT → PUSH → CLOUD
```

# 5. Setting Up Git (One‑Time)
Configure your identity (used to label commits):

```bash
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
```

Helpful settings:

```bash
# Default branch name for new repos
git config --global init.defaultBranch main

# Safer push behavior (push only current branch to its upstream)
git config --global push.default upstream

# Show nice colored output
git config --global color.ui auto
```

Verify:

```bash
git config --list
```


<!-- pagebreak -->
<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>


# 6. Starting a Project
**A) Create a brand‑new repository**
```bash
mkdir my-project
cd my-project
git init
```
Make your first commit:
```bash
echo "Hello World" > README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "Initial commit"
```
Connect to a remote later (optional):
```bash
git remote add origin https://example.com/your/repo.git
git push -u origin main
```

**B) Clone an existing repository**
```bash
git clone https://example.com/your/repo.git
cd repo
```

# 7. Making and Saving Changes (Daily Flow)
The standard edit cycle is:

1. **Edit files** in your Working Directory
2. **Stage** only what you want to commit (`git add <file>` or `git add .`)
3. **Commit** your snapshot (`git commit -m "message"`)
4. **Sync** with the team (`git pull` before pushing; resolve conflicts if needed)
5. **Push** your branch to the remote (`git push`)

Example:
```bash
# See what's changed
git status

# Stage specific file
git add src/app.js

# Commit snapshot
git commit -m "Implement search box behavior"

# Update your branch from remote, then push
git pull --rebase
git push
```

Good messages are short, imperative, and meaningful (e.g., "Fix null check on settings loader").


<!-- pagebreak -->
<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>


# 8. Branching and Merging

Branching is one of Git’s most powerful features. A **branch** is simply a pointer to a commit — an independent line of development. Branches allow safe, isolated changes before merging back into the `main` line.

A typical, correct workflow is:

1. **Modify files** in your working directory
2. **Stage** changes with `git add`
3. **Commit** with `git commit`
4. **Repeat** until ready, then merge

---

## 8.1 What Is HEAD?

In Git, **HEAD** tells you *where you are*:

- HEAD points to **the current branch** and its **latest commit**
- When you switch branches, HEAD **moves**
- When you commit, HEAD **advances** to the new commit
- HEAD determines which files are visible and **where new commits go**

See HEAD by running:

```
git status
git branch
```

Example output (the `*` indicates HEAD):

```
* myBranch
  main
```

With this in mind, let’s walk through a concrete scenario using `myFile.txt`.


<!-- pagebreak -->


## 8.2 Branching Scenario With Real File Changes

### Step 1 — Starting on `main` (before branching)

`myFile.txt` content:

```txt
Hello World.  <-- main commit #2
```

Commit graph:

```
main
 |
 o--o   <--- HEAD
```


<!-- pagebreak -->


### Step 2 — Create a feature branch from main

Command:

```
git checkout -b myBranch
```

File contents **do not change** on branch creation:

```txt
Hello World.  <-- inherited from main commit #2
```

Commit graph:

```
main
 |
 o--o

myBranch
   |
   o   <--- HEAD (myBranch)
```


<!-- pagebreak -->


### Step 3 — First change on the branch (modify → add → commit)

**Modify the file:**

```txt
Hello World.
My first change.  <-- new content added by user
```

**Stage & commit:**

```
git add myFile.txt
git commit -m "Add first change"
```

Commit graph:

```
main
 |
 o--o

myBranch
   |
   o--o   <--- HEAD (myBranch)
```


<!-- pagebreak -->


### Step 4 — Second change on the branch (modify → add → commit)

**Modify the file again:**

```txt
Hello World.
My first change.
My second change  <-- new content added by user
```

**Stage & commit:**

```
git add myFile.txt
git commit -m "Add second change"
```

Commit graph:

```
main
 |
 o--o

myBranch
   |
   o--o--o   <--- HEAD (myBranch)
```


<!-- pagebreak -->


### Step 5 — Switch back to `main` before merging

Command:

```
git checkout main
```

`main` remains unchanged:

```txt
Hello World.  <-- main commit #2
```

Commit graph:

```
main
 |
 o--o   <--- HEAD (main)

myBranch
   |
   o--o--o
```


<!-- pagebreak -->


### Step 6 — Merge the branch into `main`

Command:

```
git merge myBranch
```

Merged file on `main`:

```txt
Hello World.
My first change.
My second change  <-- main commit #3 (merge result)
```

Commit graph:

```
main
 |
 o--o------o   <--- HEAD (main)
       /
myBranch o--o--o
```

Optionally delete the feature branch:

```
git branch -d myBranch
```

---

## 8.3 Why This Matters

- All changes begin in the **working directory**
- Git records snapshots **after** you stage and commit
- Branches isolate work; `main` stays stable
- Merges integrate reviewed changes and preserve history



<!-- pagebreak -->


# 9. Undoing Mistakes (Beginner‑Safe)
- **Discard local changes to a file (not staged):**
  ```bash
  git checkout -- path/to/file
  ```
- **Unstage a file (keep edits):**
  ```bash
  git reset HEAD path/to/file
  ```
- **See history:**
  ```bash
  git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all
  ```
- **Revert a commit (create a new commit that undoes it):**
  ```bash
  git revert <commit_sha>
  ```

> Tip: Avoid `git reset --hard` until you’re comfortable; it discards changes.


<!-- pagebreak -->


# 10. Recommended Workflows
**Solo workflow**: edit → add → commit → push.  
**Team feature‑branch workflow**:
1. `git pull` to synchronize `main`
2. `git checkout -b feature/<name>`
3. Work: edit → add → commit (repeat)
4. `git push -u origin feature/<name>`
5. Open a Pull Request (PR) for review
6. Merge to `main` after approval

# 12. Summary Checklist
- Install and configure Git
- Understand the lifecycle (Untracked → Staged → Committed)
- Practice the daily flow (edit → add → commit → pull → push)
- Use branches for isolated work; merge via PRs
- Learn to read the log and recover safely
